objectives.objective: Select appropriate Claude models based on trade-offs
keyPoints: Opus: highest capability, highest cost and latency. Sonnet: balanced default for most production workloads. Haiku: fastest and cheapest for high-volume well-defined work (classification, routing, extraction, short summarization).
Choose the cheapest tier whose measured quality meets the bar — measured, via a pilot on representative data, because intuition errs in both directions.
If a blinded evaluation shows tier equivalence, the cheaper tier wins regardless of how high-stakes the domain feels.
Low-volume, high-error-cost workloads can justify Opus outright: a handful of premium requests cost less than one expensive mistake.
Mixed traffic usually beats any single tier with a routing layer — audit each workload separately.
objectives.watchFor: Extended thinking is a paid per-request dial for multi-step reasoning failures with latency slack — not a default setting, and not a fix for formatting problems.

question.stem: A blinded evaluation on representative medical-billing records shows Sonnet and Opus performing equivalently on a high-volume coding task. The team argues Opus is safer because the domain is regulated. What should the architect recommend?
options: Opus, because regulated domains warrant maximum capability
Sonnet, since measured quality is equivalent and the premium buys nothing on this workload
Opus with extended thinking enabled to further reduce risk
Alternate between tiers and compare production error rates over time
question.answerWhy: Tier choice is an economic decision constrained by measured quality, so demonstrated equivalence means the premium is unfunded — domain stakes are not evidence. Adding extended thinking compounds cost and latency for a reasoning failure the evaluation did not find, and alternating tiers in production introduces variance where a controlled evaluation already answered the question.

objectives.objective: Design system prompts, templates, and guardrails
keyPoints: Separate what never changes from what changes per request: one versioned system prompt for stable instructions, template variables for per-request data in the user turn.
Delimit sections with XML tags; wrap untrusted input in labeled tags and instruct the model to treat tagged content as data to analyze, never as instructions.
Ordering: long documents first, instructions and question last, so the task sits adjacent to where generation happens.
Guardrails need deterministic validation outside the model — instructions inside it shift probabilities, they do not guarantee.
Resolve contradictory instructions at the source through ownership and review, not with a precedence meta-rule.
objectives.watchFor: Interleaving per-request data with stable instructions in one generated blob makes prompts unreviewable, drift-prone, and uncacheable all at once.

question.stem: Three teams have added rules to a shared system prompt, and two of them now contradict each other. What should the architect do?
options: Add a precedence meta-rule stating which team's rules take priority
Assign ownership and resolve the conflict at the source by deleting or scoping the losing rule
Move the conflicting rules to the end of the prompt where the model attends most closely
Split the prompt so each team's rules are applied in a separate model call
question.answerWhy: Model behaviour under contradiction is undefined, so the only reliable fix is removing the contradiction — which requires an owner and a review path. A precedence rule papers over the conflict, repositioning it only shifts probabilities, and splitting into separate calls multiplies cost while leaving both rules in force somewhere.

objectives.objective: Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
keyPoints: An escalation ladder — stop at the lowest rung meeting the quality bar, because each rung taxes every request in tokens and latency.
Zero-shot with clear instructions is the starting point; capable models handle most well-specified tasks without demonstrations.
Few-shot (typically 3–5 examples) pins down rigid output formats and edge-case handling better than prose descriptions.
Example quality and diversity beat quantity — the set defines the expected input distribution, so include the messy production cases.
Chain-of-thought targets multi-step reasoning failures where latency has slack, and the reasoning must precede the answer.
objectives.watchFor: Each technique targets a different failure mode — chain-of-thought does not fix formatting and few-shot does not fix reasoning depth. Large homogeneous example sets inflate cost and overfit to incidental quirks.

question.stem: An extraction prompt uses 22 examples, all clean single-item invoices. It handles those perfectly but fails on multi-item records and missing fields. What is the best revision?
options: Add another dozen examples covering more invoice variations
Cut to a small diverse set that includes multi-item records and missing fields, and add chain-of-thought reasoning
Replace the example set with 3–5 examples that span the edge cases, including multi-item and missing-field records
Keep the examples and add an instruction to handle multi-item and incomplete invoices carefully
question.answerWhy: The example set defines the input distribution the model expects, so the fix is diversity over volume: a handful of examples that demonstrate the failing edge cases. Adding more happy-path examples inflates cost while overfitting further, chain-of-thought targets reasoning rather than unseen formats, and an instruction cannot demonstrate what the examples never showed.

objectives.objective: Optimize context windows and manage token usage
keyPoints: Capacity is not a reason to fill it — accuracy degrades as context fills with irrelevant content through attention dilution and similar-but-wrong passages.
Retrieving the few relevant sections at request time beats dumping an entire corpus, even when the corpus fits.
Long interactions need structured summarization — distil goals, decisions, and open items and carry that forward with recent turns; naive truncation discards the durable facts coherence depends on.
Agentic workflows need context hygiene: filter each tool result to what is relevant before it enters the conversation, and compact older exchanges.
Profile the token budget and attack the dominant term — usually machine-generated input data, not the instructions.
objectives.watchFor: Leaving max output tokens at defaults silently truncates exactly the largest, most complex responses — size the limit from measured worst-case output.

question.stem: A long-running assistant starts contradicting decisions from earlier in the session. The team currently truncates the conversation to the most recent turns. What should replace this?
options: Periodic structured summarization capturing goals, decisions, and open items, carried forward with recent turns
Resending the full transcript each turn now that the context window is large
Truncating to a larger number of recent turns
Moving to a model with a larger context window
question.answerWhy: Truncation discards precisely the durable state — goals and prior decisions — that coherence depends on, which is why structured summarization carried alongside recent turns is the standard remedy. Resending the whole transcript becomes impractical and dilutes attention, and both a longer truncation window and a bigger context window postpone the failure without preserving the decisions.

objectives.objective: Implement prompt reuse strategies (caching, modular prompts, Skills)
keyPoints: Caching is strict prefix matching — the cache hits only when the prompt's beginning is byte-for-byte identical, so any change anywhere in the prefix invalidates it.
Design stable-first, variable-last, with the breakpoint at the boundary so only stable content forms the cached prefix.
The short TTL (about five minutes) refreshes on each use, so steady traffic and sequential batches keep prefixes warm; content seen once should never be cached.
Share rules as a single versioned module composed into each assistant's prompt at build time — copy-paste duplication guarantees drift and eventual policy contradictions.
Package occasional-use procedures as Skills loaded on demand instead of keeping them resident in every prompt.
objectives.watchFor: A misplaced timestamp or session ID ahead of the stable content silently zeroes every cache read while the billing looks superficially normal.

question.stem: A team enabled prompt caching on a large stable policy corpus but sees no cost reduction. Each prompt begins with a generated request timestamp. What is happening?
options: The five-minute TTL expires between requests, so entries never get reused
The timestamp sits ahead of the stable content, so the prefix never matches and every request pays a cache write
The corpus exceeds the maximum cacheable prefix size
Caching only reduces output token cost, which this workload barely uses
question.answerWhy: Caching matches on an exact prefix, so a value that changes every request placed before the stable corpus guarantees a miss and repeated write premiums. The TTL refreshes on use so steady traffic stays warm, and neither a size limit nor an output-cost misconception explains a prefix that is different on every call.
